query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Aluminum additions in ferritic/martensitic ODS steels promote the formation of a continuous, Al2O3-containing passive film that retards oxygen ingress and dissolution-based corrosion in high-temperature liquid Pb environments.
generation.material_initial_state: 9Cr ODS steel with a baseline low Al content exhibiting discontinuous Cr-rich oxide films.
generation.intervention: Introduce controlled Al additions (e.g., form 9CrAl ODS steel) during alloy processing.
generation.conditions: Expose samples to liquid Pb at 600 °C for up to 2000 hours under controlled oxygen concentrations (~10^–6 wt.%).
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, dense alumina (Al2O3)-containing oxide scale that forms uniformly on the surface.
generation.mechanism: Al, having a high oxygen affinity, lowers the thermodynamic barrier for Al2O3 formation; the continuous film impedes both oxygen ingress and metal dissolution compared to discontinuous Cr-oxide scales.
generation.predicted_outcome: 9CrAl ODS steel will exhibit approximately 40% reduced maximum corrosion depth relative to conventional 9Cr ODS steel, along with more uniform oxide scale morphology.
generation.baseline: 9Cr ODS steel without significant Al addition under identical exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: Valid for high-temperature liquid metal conditions (around 600 °C) and controlled low-oxygen content environments; may not apply at lower temperatures or in non-liquid metal media.
generation.uncertainty: Potential interactions with fine-grain structure effects and possible local dissolution phenomena not wholly mitigated by Al addition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of ODS steel samples: one with standard 9Cr ODS composition and one with added Al to form 9CrAl ODS. Expose both sets to liquid Pb at 600 °C for 2000 hours under identical oxygen-controlled conditions.
measurements: Cross-sectional SEM and EDS analysis to quantify corrosion layer thickness and uniformity.
Weight gain measurements to compare oxide scale formation kinetics.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the 9CrAl ODS samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction (>30–40%) in maximum corrosion depth or uniformity of the passive film compared with the baseline 9Cr ODS, then the hypothesis that Al additions improve corrosion resistance via in situ Al2O3 film formation would be falsified.

Compared with other corrosive media, such as high-temperature water or gas, the liquid metal in lead-based reactors has serious dissolution corrosion to structural materials at high temperature, especially the elements of Ni and Cr []. The T91 ferritic/martensitic steel does not contain Ni and has a lower content of Cr compared to austenitic steels and, therefore, is considered an important candidate for lead-cooled reactors. However, the working temperature of traditional ferritic/martensitic steel is usually below 550–600 °C, which cannot meet the service requirements of the future lead-cooled reactor. If introducing very fine oxide particles with a high number density into the matrix of steel, the operation temperature can be increased to 700 °C []. A thin local distributed layer with a thickness of 1 micron can be found along the original boundary, which separated the corrosion layer and Pb attached to the surface of the sample. EDS results show that this layer was rich in Cr and O elements, and the distribution of Cr and O is consistent, indicating that it was an oxide film rich in Cr2O3. However, this film is not continuous and dense enough due to the low Cr content of the material; therefore, it cannot play a protective role for the long-term corrosion resistance. This is consistent with the reported results of 9Cr ODS steel in flowing LBE. Under the condition of 10−6 wt% oxygen concentration, IOZ internal oxidation was always formed []. papers.title: Comparison of Corrosion Behavior of T91, 9Cr and 9CrAl ODS Steels in Liquid Pb.
papers.system: Ferritic/martensitic steels (T91, 9Cr ODS, 9CrAl ODS) used in lead-cooled reactor environments
papers.approach: Long-term exposure tests in liquid Pb at 600 °C (up to 2000 h) with microstructural and surface analyses (SEM, EDS) to compare different alloy formulations
papers.findings: 9CrAl ODS steel exhibited a significant reduction in maximum corrosion depth (approximately 51.8 μm vs thicker scales in others). T91 formed complex oxidation products and nonuniform oxide layers, while 9Cr ODS had localized Cr2O3 films that were discontinuous due to limited Cr content and fine-grained dissolution effects.
papers.mechanism: The addition of Al promotes formation of a continuous and stable Al2O3-containing oxide film that retards both oxygen ingress and diffusion-driven dissolution of alloy elements. Fine-grain structures also modulate the corrosion kinetics.

papers.title: Effect of Silicon on Dynamic/Static Corrosion Resistance of T91 in Lead-Bismuth Eutectic at 550 °C.
papers.system: T91 ferritic/martensitic steel in lead–bismuth eutectic (LBE) environments typical of nuclear reactor coolants
papers.approach: Systematic variation of Si content (0.5, 1.3, and 2.0 wt.%) in T91 steel with tests conducted under dynamic (flowing) and static LBE conditions at 550 °C; characterization via XRD, SEM, TEM, and EPMA
papers.findings: Raising the Si content, with an optimum near 1.3 wt.%, led to the formation of a thinner and more stable oxide film. The Si-rich oxide localized near the inner oxide layer promoted subsequent Cr oxide formation in the internal oxidation zone, thereby enhancing corrosion resistance.
papers.mechanism: Si lowers the Gibbs free energy for oxide formation, directly influencing the kinetics of oxide layer growth and improving the stability and protective quality of the passive film through modified wettability and diffusion pathways.

papers.title: Corrosion Behavior of Alumina-Forming Austenitic Steel in Supercritical Carbon Dioxide Conditions: Effects of Nb Content and Temperature.
papers.system: Alumina-forming austenitic (AFA) stainless steels aimed at high-temperature, high-pressure environments (e.g., advanced nuclear or chemical process systems) in supercritical CO2
papers.approach: Exposure tests in supercritical CO2 at 500 °C and 600 °C under 20 MPa, with variations in Nb content to study its effect on oxide scale structure, complemented by weight gain measurements and microstructural analysis (SEM, TEM)
papers.findings: An initially formed duplex oxide layer consisting of an outer Cr2O3 film and inner Al2O3 layer (with interspersed Fe-rich spinels) provided superior corrosion resistance at an optimal Nb addition (~0.6 wt.%). Excessive Nb resulted in thicker, continuous Fe-rich nodules and internal oxide zones, diminishing performance.
papers.mechanism: Nb modulates diffusion kinetics and grain boundary characteristics to promote the formation of a protective dual-oxide scale. The controlled diffusion of Cr and Al through refined grain boundaries is central to forming a dense, adherent film that limits further corrosion.

papers.title: Corrosion behavior of metastable AISI 321 austenitic stainless steel: Investigating the effect of grain size and prior plastic deformation on its degr
papers.system: AISI 321 austenitic stainless steel used in chemical-processing environments
papers.approach: Thermomechanical processing to generate coarse (~37 μm), fine (~3 μm), and ultrafine (~0.24 μm) grained structures; samples were subjected to dynamic and quasi-static deformation and then exposed to 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution, with electrochemical and microstructural characterization
papers.findings: Ultrafine-grained specimens exhibited the highest corrosion resistance due to the formation of a more stable, adsorbed passive film. Additionally, corrosion resistance was superior in quasi-statically deformed samples compared to dynamically deformed or undeformed ones.
papers.mechanism: Grain refinement enhances the density of grain boundaries which act as sites for forming a protective passive film. However, deformation conditions influence texture and passivation characteristics, with quasi-static loading better promoting the formation of protective crystallographic orientations.

papers.title: Long-Term Corrosion Behavior of Strong and Ductile High Mn-Low Cr Steel in Acidic Aqueous Environments.
papers.system: High Mn-low Cr steel intended for chemical processing where acidic aqueous environments prevail
papers.approach: Long-term immersion tests combined with electrochemical measurements (linear polarization resistance, impedance) and metallographic observations to compare corrosion behavior with conventional ferritic steels
papers.findings: Although the high Mn-low Cr steel initially exhibited lower corrosion resistance (with higher corrosion current density), its resistance improved over time due to the gradual formation of a (Fe, Cr)-enriched oxide scale that provided enhanced protection compared to conventional steels.
papers.mechanism: The slow kinetics associated with the formation of a protective oxide scale under acidic conditions eventually leads to densification and selective enrichment of corrosion-resistant elements, thus enhancing the long-term corrosion resistance.

established: Adding alloying elements like Al and Si can promote the formation of dense, protective oxide layers (e.g., Al2O3, Cr2O3) that mitigate corrosion in high-temperature and aggressive environments.
Refined grain structures and controlled thermomechanical treatments enhance passive film stability and overall corrosion resistance.
Optimizing element concentrations (such as Si in T91 or Nb in AFA steels) is critical to balancing oxide film properties and minimizing detrimental phases.

approaches_tried.approach: Introducing fine oxide dispersion particles (ODS) and Al additions in ferritic/martensitic steels to form protective alumina layers.
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved high-temperature corrosion resistance in liquid Pb environments; reduction in corrosion depth; record_ids: [PMC10054900::web::002::1_introduction, PMC10054900::web::023::4_conclusions].

approaches_tried.approach: Varying Si content in T91 steel to modify oxide film composition and structure.
approaches_tried.outcome: Optimal Si content (around 1.3 wt.%) produced thinner, more stable oxide films and enhanced corrosion resistance in LBE environments; record_ids: [PMC9028533::web::000::abstract, PMC9028533::web::023::4_discussion].

approaches_tried.approach: Adding Nb to alumina-forming austenitic steels to adjust diffusion kinetics and oxide layer formation under supercritical CO2 conditions.
approaches_tried.outcome: An optimal Nb addition (~0.6 wt.%) yielded a duplex oxide scale with improved protection, though higher Nb proved detrimental; record_ids: [PMC10254796::web::002::1_introduction, PMC10254796::web::035::5_conclusions].

approaches_tried.approach: Thermomechanical processing (grain refinement and deformation rate variation) of AISI 321 stainless steel.
approaches_tried.outcome: Ultrafine grains and quasi-static deformation led to enhanced passive film stability and improved corrosion resistance in saline environments; record_ids: [PMC6702197::web::023::effect_of_grain_size_on_corrosion_resist, PMC6702197::web::036::conclusions].

mechanisms: Formation of continuous and protective oxide films (e.g., Al2O3, Cr2O3) that hinder oxygen diffusion and elemental dissolution.
Diffusion control at refined grain boundaries promoting rapid passivation.
Alloying-induced modification of oxidation kinetics, where elements like Si and Nb alter the thermodynamics and kinetics of oxide layer formation.
disagreements: The effect of grain refinement can be double-edged: while it promotes passivation, an increased grain boundary area may also accelerate dissolution under certain conditions.

Excessive addition of elements (e.g., too much Nb) can lead to the formation of detrimental phases or non-protective oxide morphologies, in contrast to the beneficial effects seen at optimal concentrations.
open_questions: How do these protective mechanisms behave under simultaneous exposure to high-temperature, corrosive liquid metals and irradiation conditions typical of nuclear reactor environments?
What is the interplay between microstructural features induced by thermomechanical processing and alloying additions during long-term service in coupled corrosive/irradiative environments?
Can controlled grain-boundary engineering and optimized alloy chemistry be combined to further enhance corrosion resistance without compromising mechanical properties?
opportunities: Designing controlled studies that combine optimal alloying (e.g., balanced Al, Si, and Nb additions) with targeted grain refinement to decouple the role of oxide film formation vs. diffusion kinetics in corrosion resistance under nuclear reactor conditions.
Extending corrosion testing to environments that simulate both high temperature and irradiation, thereby mimicking the actual service conditions in nuclear power applications.

Investigating the use of in situ techniques (e.g., advanced spectroscopy and imaging) to probe the evolution and stability of protective oxide layers on steels during exposure to liquid metal coolants or supercritical CO2.

directions.direction: Alloy design via aluminum additions to promote in situ formation of a continuous alumina-based passive film in ODS steels.
directions.assessment: Directly addresses corrosion resistance by enhancing oxide film stability in high-temperature liquid metal environments. Well supported by evidence from studies on 9CrAl ODS steels, though grain effects may complicate the outcome.

directions.direction: Optimization of Si content in T91 steels to modify the oxide film’s composition and structure, thereby stabilizing the passive layer in lead–bismuth environments.
directions.assessment: Targets oxide film thickness and stability through controlled alloying. Evidence shows an optimum around 1.3 wt.% Si, making this approach both feasible and mechanistically supported.

directions.direction: Thermomechanical grain refinement in austenitic stainless steels (e.g., AISI 321) to increase grain boundary density and promote rapid, stable passive film formation.
directions.assessment: Alters the kinetic route of passivation by increasing nucleation sites. While enhanced grain boundaries can accelerate diffusion sometimes, the passive film improvement under moderate corrosion conditions is well documented.

directions.direction: Nb microalloying in alumina-forming austenitic (AFA) steels to tune grain boundary diffusion and facilitate optimal duplex oxide (Cr2O3/Al2O3) scale formation in supercritical CO2 conditions.
directions.assessment: Directly tests diffusion‐mediated oxide formation; studies indicate an optimum Nb level (around 0.6 wt.%) enhances oxidation resistance, but excessive Nb is detrimental. Feasible within defined high-temperature/pressure conditions.

directions.direction: Low-temperature plasma nitriding in stainless steels to adjust near-surface composition without Cr depletion, thereby influencing passive film characteristics.
directions.assessment: Addresses surface passivation and wear–corrosion balance, yet the risk of forming Cr-nitrides makes the mechanism less straightforward for nuclear and aggressive chemical environments.

candidates.hypothesis: Grain refinement in AISI 321 austenitic stainless steel enhances corrosion resistance by increasing grain boundary density, which accelerates the formation of a uniform and stable passive film in chloride-containing environments.
candidates.intervention: Apply thermomechanical processing to produce fine (~3 µm) and ultrafine (~0.24 µm) grained structures, with additional quasi-static deformation to promote favorable crystallographic orientations.

candidates.hypothesis: In alumina-forming austenitic steels, the addition of ~0.6 wt.% Nb refines grain boundary diffusion pathways, promoting the formation of an optimal duplex oxide scale (outer Cr2O3 and inner Al2O3) that significantly enhances corrosion resistance in supercritical CO2 environments.
